facts.statement: The genus Pterichthyodes was described by Bleeker in 1859.
The type species of the genus is Pterichthyodes milleri.
Pterichthyodes belongs to the family Asterolepididae.
Pterichthyodes is classified within the order Antiarchi.
Pterichthyodes lived during the Devonian period.
facts.quote: Pterichthyodes is a genus of antiarch placoderm fishes from the Devonian period.

facts.statement: Pterichthyodes lived from the Eifelian to the Givetian stages, between 393.47 and 382.31 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Eifelian to Givetian (393.47 to 382.31 million years ago)

facts.statement: Fossils of Pterichthyodes have been found in Scotland.
facts.quote: Its fossils have been discovered in Scotland.

facts.statement: Pterichthyodes had heavily armored heads and forebodies but unarmored, scaly tails.
facts.quote: As with all other antiarchs, Pterichthyodes had heavily armored heads and forebodies, while their scaly tails were unarmored.

facts.statement: Specimens of Pterichthyodes ranged in length from 8 to 12 inches.
facts.quote: Specimen length ranges from 8 in to 12 in.

facts.statement: As placoderms, Pterichthyodes were among the earliest vertebrates to possess jaws, but they had grinding plates instead of teeth.
facts.quote: As placoderms, they were members of the earliest known vertebrates to possess jaws, though they had grinding plates rather than teeth.

facts.statement: The name Pterichthyodes refers to the genus's unique wing-like appendages.
facts.quote: The generic name of Pterichthyodes refers directly to their odd wing-like appendages

facts.statement: Fossils suggest Pterichthyodes was a bottom-dweller that crawled on lake beds using its pectoral appendages.
facts.quote: Fossils of Pterichtyodes showing eyes positioned on the direct of the head and a "ventrally flattened trunk shield" suggest that it was a "bottom dweller", living at the bottom of lakes, where it might have crawled using its pectoral appendages.

facts.statement: It is theorized that Pterichthyodes used its appendages to bury itself in the sediment.
facts.quote: It has also been theorized that Pterichthyodes and other antiarchs used these appendages to bury itself.

facts.statement: Pterichthyodes likely fed by browsing shallow lake beds for decaying detritus.
facts.quote: Pterichthyodes would have fed by browsing shallower areas of the lake bed for decaying detritus.

facts.statement: Found specimens of Pterichthyodes range from 20 to 30 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: Las longitudes de los especímenes hallados van desde 20 centímetros hasta 30 centímetros.

facts.statement: Pterichthyodes is easily distinguished from other placoderms by its strange wing-shaped appendages.
facts.quote: Pterichthyodes se distingue fácilmente de otros placodermos por sus extraños apéndices en forma de ala

facts.statement: Pterichthyodes may have fed by moving through shallow lake beds searching for decaying detritus.
facts.quote: Pterichthyodes pudo haberse alimentado navegando por las áreas poco profundidad de los lechos de lagos buscando el detritus en descomposición.

facts.statement: Pterichthyodes was one of the first species recognized as distinct, with fossils common in the Old Red Sandstone formation studied since the early 19th century.
facts.quote: They were one of the first species recognized for what they were, as their fossils are common in the Old Red Sandstone formation studied by geologists in the early 19th century.

facts.statement: Pterichthyodes remained an unsolved puzzle due to its extreme divergence from modern fish until Charles Darwin proposed evolutionary theories.
facts.quote: Due to their extreme divergence from modern-day fish, they were a puzzle unsolved until Charles Darwin brought forward his theories on evolution.
